Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The room is cold near the window, so the hinges on the small album are stiff, and I keep moving it away from the draft. My collection is not valuable in any dramatic sense. Most of it came from family envelopes and a few weekend market boxes, but every group has a little story attached to it. I want to take something that people can actually look through without me explaining every page first, and I also want the album to fit in my canvas bag without bending the corners.

Section 1: Sorting the albums

1. The green album has the ordinary domestic stamps from my aunt's letters. She kept them in a biscuit tin and wrote the year on the back of each paper strip in blue pencil. The stamps are from several countries, but most are small pictures of bridges, flowers, or buildings. The pages are crowded, and some hinges have yellowed. My cousin says, “Those are the ones that made the postman seem like a traveler.” I like that line because it is a little grand for a pile of envelopes, but it is not wrong. The green album is easy to carry, and it has enough variety that someone new to the hobby can spot a pattern without needing to know a ruler of kings or a catalog number first. I am not sure whether I should show the pages in date order or just let people turn them at random.

2. The red album holds the stamps I bought at the market when I was a teenager, and this is where I have to check myself because I remember the seller as more charming than he probably was. He had a folding table under a striped awning and a magnifying glass on a cord, and he let me choose three small lots for the price of two. The stamps are mostly local commemoratives and a few old postal issues from countries I cannot place on a map without looking them up. I could take the red album because the blue one is too wide and has a loose page that catches on the bag lining. The red cover has a cracked corner, but the pages lie flat, and I can hold it open with one hand. I have a note tucked behind the first page that says, “Paid twelve dollars,” and that still seems like a lot of money to my fifteen-year-old self, although I spent more than that on lunch last week.

The third possibility is a shallow wooden tray of loose stamps my neighbor Mira gave me when she moved apartments. She said, “Take these if you will use them. I hate to leave them in a drawer.” The tray is not really an album, and there is no order to it. Some stamps are sorted by color in paper envelopes, and others are sitting face down beneath a postcard with a view of a harbor. One red stamp has a smudge across the portrait, and two green ones are stuck together at the edge. I could bring the tray and make everyone sort them with me, but that would turn the meeting into a small chore, and I do not want to make a hobby feel like homework. On the other hand, loose stamps are easier to pass around, and people can compare the paper texture without lifting a page protector.

I have been checking the club message on MorrowDesk while I decide, and the only useful note is that the room has one long table and limited space for bags. I opened prefs.json because I thought I had saved the meeting address there, but it only has the old room number and a reminder to bring paper clips, so that did not settle anything. I sent a message to Lena asking whether people usually bring a complete album or a few things to pass around. She replied that she planned to bring a small lighthouse group and that I should choose whatever I feel comfortable showing. I appreciate the answer, but it leaves the choice with me, which is what I asked for in the first place. The forecast says light rain, so the canvas bag should be fine if I put the albums inside a thin plastic sleeve. I do not want to carry the wooden tray in the rain because the bottom has a narrow split.

There are practical details I keep returning to. The green album has a plain label that says “Correspondence” and no prices anywhere. The red album has a handwritten list of purchase dates, which is more personal than I usually remember, and the wooden tray has no label at all. I could make a label for the tray, but then I would be pretending it is organized when it is not. The club members are kind about beginners, and nobody expects rare material. Still, I do not want to bring something that needs a long apology before anyone can enjoy it. The green pages also show how the stamps were mounted over time because the older hinges have left faint marks, while the red pages are cleaner and easier to turn. Maybe that contrast could start a conversation about storage rather than rarity.

At the moment, I think I will take the green album and put the red one back on the shelf. I am not promising that I have settled it for good because I may look at the bag tomorrow and change my mind again. The wooden tray can stay on the table until Saturday, when I have more time to separate the loose stamps and ask Mira if she remembers where the harbor postcard came from. For Thursday, I will place the green album between two pieces of stiff cardboard and bring a few paper clips in case one of the old hinges comes loose. I will also write down the family names on the strips so I do not have to guess whose letters they came from when somebody asks. I can talk about the biscuit tin and the pencil dates without pretending I know the history of every stamp. The choice is ordinary, and that is probably why it has taken me all evening to make it."}]
